summary: SE-led troubleshooting on KV cache eviction and prefix reuse behavior. Identified likely paging/eviction due to mixed short/long contexts and suboptimal per-shard cache sizing; discussed bypassing eviction with LRU tuning, reserved KV pages, and preferrable routing to dedicated hosts. Agreed on bench plan and next steps.
transcript:
Meeting header:
- Date/time: 2027-02-10 15:00 UTC
- Duration: ~62 minutes
- Attendees: Carlos (Redwood AE), Priya (Redwood SE), Ethan (Redwood SRE), Aisha (Novus CTO), Ben (Novus ML), Samir (Novus Platform), Lina (Novus Data)

00:00 Priya: okay thanks everyone for joining uh we'll be focused on the kv cache eviction and prefix reuse pattern you reported, we pulled the logs and a couple of configs beforehand so we can walk through, feel free to jump in
00:18 Aisha: sounds good, thanks. just to reiterate main pain is p95 spikes when some sessions go to 5k tokens then come back to short chats and we see cache churn and higher cost, yes
00:35 Ben: and sometimes we see weird prefix misses even when the prompt prefix is identical, so i'm worried keys are colliding or getting evicted mid-session
00:48 Priya: right, two things to call out early: first eviction vs paging difference - eviction is proactive removal due to size/LRU, paging is when we move cold kv pages out to slower storage for long-context supports; second prefix reuse can be impacted by hash sharding and tokenization differences
01:10 Carlos: quick context from our side - Novus is on Dedicated nodes with mixed short and long sessions. you mentioned using 2xA100-like shapes with nvlink, is that right Samir?
01:24 Samir: yes 2xA100 per host, we have 8 shard replicas across cluster, each shard handles subset of sessions, memory limits per shard are set to 40GB in the runtime config. we do per-tenant KV allocation via reservation but it might be coarse
01:42 Priya: okay that matters a lot. eviction pressure often comes from per-shard allocation being too low for the long tail of long-context sessions. can you share the eviction counts and page-in rates?
01:56 Samir: we pulled a sample: eviction_count spikes to ~12k/min during mixed-workload windows, page_in rate also climbs and we see >30% requests hitting page-in which correlates with latency spikes
02:15 Ethan: one red flag is the per-request batching behavior. when you batch many short requests together we keep growing kv usage because prefixes from different sessions get coalesced in the same batch and pin pages longer than expected
02:30 Ben: hmm we do use dynamic batching with 4-8 request batch target, intended to improve throughput, but i didn't think it would increase retention like that
02:42 Priya: it can, especially if your batch window is large and you have a mix of seq lengths. two mitigations: reduce max batch window for low-latency routes, or enable per-session isolation in batching (prefetch/pin controls) so short sessions don't inherit long-session pages
03:05 Lina: about prefix misses: we saw the tokenized prefix sometimes has invisible whitespace variants from our client, am i right that normalizing tokenization helps?
03:14 Priya: yes normalization first. also watch for model-specific tokenizer differences; even minor variant leads to different cache keys. we recommend canonicalization at the app layer and include normalized hash in session metadata
03:29 Ben: what about key collision or sharding skew? we have 8 shards and i noticed some shards are 2-3x hotter
03:38 Priya: shard skew can be from naive hash modulus with non-uniform prefixes. consider consistent hashing or adding salt per-session to distribute keys. but salt changes keys, so for reuse you want stable mapping; instead use a better hash function and consider virtual nodes to smooth load
03:55 Carlos: mart, can you show the quick heuristic we use for reserved pages per-tenant?
04:01 Marta: sure, the heuristic is a percentile-based reservation: reserve pages proportional to the 95th percentile of per-session kv usage observed over a rolling window, with a floor to protect small tenants. we also have burst tokens to allow short-term overage without eviction
04:22 Samir: we don't currently compute 95th percentile per-tenant, it's global. that's likely why we see tenants with longer contexts evicting others
04:30 Priya: yep switch to per-tenant or per-route reservation thresholds to avoid noisy neighbors. also enable soft reservations for routes used for long-context retrieval so they're less likely to be paged out
04:45 Ben: curious about paging to disk  we run on-prem with local NVMe, what are performance tradeoffs vs keeping everything in memory?
04:53 Priya: paging gives you ability to support very long contexts but at cost of page-in latency. with NVMe and asynchronous prefetching you can keep p95 reasonable, but p99 suffers. with NVLink and unified memory options you can offload less frequently used KV segments to remote shared memory across GPUs which helps if network is fast
05:18 Ethan: we also saw quantization reduced model memory but didn't help kv size much, any thoughts?
05:24 Priya: quantization mostly affects model weights, kv cache is about activations and key/value tensors; certain quant formats can shrink kv values but gains are modest. consider sparse KV compression or smaller dtype for cache values when acceptable (float16 -> int8 tradeoffs), but must validate model quality
05:42 Aisha: for private deployment, what about KMS or audit traces for kv data? do we need to worry about encryption in cache?
05:50 Carlos: Redwood supports in-memory encrypted KV with customer-managed keys in Private mode; audit logs can be emitted for page-in/page-out and eviction events tied to session ids
06:04 Lina: back to reproducible prefix reuse - is there way to force reuse by marking session keys explicit?
06:12 Priya: yes we expose an optional session_kv_id in the API; if your app sets a stable session_kv_id for conversation threads we will use that as primary key which greatly improves reuse. caveat: if multiple sessions share id they'll share kv state so only use for single logical thread
06:28 Ben: what's the recommended shard sizing math? we currently do 40GB per shard, but maybe we need more headroom
06:34 Priya: rough rule: provision for 1.5x the 95th percentile of per-session kv usage * expected concurrent sessions per shard. if you have long tails provision more aggressively or use dedicated long-context hosts with larger per-shard mem
06:50 Samir: can Redwood help with an automated rebalancer? shard hot spotting is a pain for us
06:56 Priya: we have an internal balancer that can migrate session ownership and rehash virtual nodes, but for Dedicated customers we can run the rebalancer in read-only advisory mode first so you can sanity check moves
07:12 Ben: any quick config flags we can flip now to reduce evictions?
07:18 Priya: yes - lower eviction aggressiveness (set eviction_target_ratio to 0.85), raise reserved_pages for long-context routes, enable per-session_kv_id, and reduce max_batch_window to 8ms for your low-latency routes. those are safe to toggle in staging
07:36 Aisha: awesome can we get those exact config snippets?
07:40 Priya: i'll share the doc, yes. i'll also include a small Lua-ish snippet for example runtime.yml override
07:49 Carlos: we should talk about benchmark plan  Samir, Ben, do you prefer we run with synthetic input or replay production traces?
07:56 Samir: we can do both; replay is ideal for fidelity but we need to scrub pii first. we'll start with a 24h sampled replay and run synthetic for stress tests at 5k and 10k token sequences
08:10 Ben: for metrics we'll capture eviction_count, page_in_rate, p95/p99 latency, kv_hit_ratio, and batch_wait_ms
08:20 Priya: perfect, also gather per-shard heatmaps and tokenization diffs for prefixes
08:28 Lina: question  is there a risk enabling session_kv_id for millions of sessions causing growth?
08:33 Priya: it increases number of distinct entries, yes, but if you have ephemeral threads you can set ttl on session_kv_id or use ephemeral ids; TTL and soft-evict help manage cardinality
08:48 Aisha: if we move to Redwood Private completely, will network overhead to KMS or audit affect latency?
08:55 Carlos: KMS calls are async for kv store encryption; we cache keys on the host so runtime impact is minimal. audit logs buffer and flush in batches to avoid tail latency effects
09:10 Ben: last question  any gotchas with tokenizer version mismatches across models that cause false misses?
09:16 Priya: yes, using two models with different tokenizers means cache keys are incompatible. if you're routing between model variants for cost reasons, ensure you either re-tokenize or scope cache per-model-variant. we usually include model_id in cache key metadata
09:36 Carlos: ok let's recap next steps and owners
09:40 Priya: recap: share docs/config (Priya), Novus to run replay + synthetic bench and share logs (Samir/Ben), Redwood to run a follow-up bench with our long-context hosts and same trace (Priya/Ethan). meet again after results
09:56 Aisha: thanks everyone, useful session
10:02 Carlos: thanks all, we'll send notes and config by EOD, talk soon
10:15 (call ends)

Notes: transcript contains minor transcription artifacts and some overlapping speaker labels; timestamps approximate. The runtime config keys mentioned are representative, not exact; Redwood SE will attach a config snippet and detailed eviction telemetry dashboard link in follow up.
